title: Evolutionary theodicy
summary:
Evolutionary theodicies attempt to reconcile the problem of animal suffering and natural evil with the existence of an all-good, all-powerful God. Proponents argue that a universe with the complexity, beauty, and diversity found on Earth could only come about through the natural, evolutionary processes of competition, predation, and death. Consequently, the goodness of creation is viewed as inextricably linked to the pain required to produce it. 

Theodicists like Christopher Southgate suggest that God suffers alongside all creatures and that these evolutionary costs are justified by greater goods, such as creaturely freedom and unique individual existence. Furthermore, many proponents invoke eschatology, arguing that all animals will eventually experience divine fulfillment and redemption. Critics, however, object to the perceived constraints on divine power, the integration of violence into creation, and the necessity of such suffering.

title: Execution ballad
summary:
Execution ballads were popular street literature across Europe from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries, with some produced until World War II. Sold as broadsides and pamphlets by roving vendors, these songs detailed the lives, crimes, and executions of criminals. They typically served as cautionary tales, portraying the condemned as guilty and remorseful, and were often written from the criminal's perspective as a final warning to the public. 

Because many people were illiterate, music helped spread the news. Ballads usually lacked original musical notation, instead instructing singers to use the tunes of popular songs or hymns. Formats and styles varied by region, covering religious persecution, witchcraft, and eventually focusing heavily on murders, continuing in some areas even after public executions ended.

title: Ancient Roman symbols of monetary and weight units
summary:
Symbols for ancient Roman monetary and weight units—such as the denarius, sestertius, and libra—originated during the late Roman Republic. They appeared both on coins and in written documents, occasionally surviving into modern times. These symbols were generally formed using modified Roman numerals, Greek letters, counting dots or strokes, or abbreviations of unit names. 

In everyday and business correspondence, such as the Vindolanda tablets, currency symbols were frequently placed before numerical amounts, a convention still used today by certain modern currencies. Furthermore, many ancient Roman units heavily influenced subsequent European, Asian, and African monetary and weight systems. For example, the libra, solidus, and denarius inspired numerous later coins and units, including the British £sd system, which endured into the 20th century.

title: Women in Eritrea
summary:
Eritrean women have historically played vital roles in both labor and warfare. During the 30-year War for Independence, women comprised about one-third of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF), serving in combat alongside men and challenging traditional gender roles. Influenced by Marxist-Leninist ideology, the EPLF instituted progressive reforms, including marriage laws that banned dowries and child marriage. However, because female fighters were often treated like men rather than supported in their female identities, these gains largely dissolved after the war. 

In daily life, Eritrean women contribute heavily to agriculture, food storage, and fishing, frequently working longer hours than men. While elementary school teaching positions have equal gender representation, women face educational barriers due to early marriage, cultural expectations, and long travel distances to secondary schools.

title: Fire accelerant
summary: A fire accelerant, or ignitable liquid, is any substance that burns rapidly to increase the speed, temperature, and heat release rate of a fire. While accelerants are frequently used to commit arson, fire investigators may also use the term without implying criminal intent. Most accelerants are flammable liquids or hydrocarbon-based fuels, including gasoline, kerosene, diesel fuel, turpentine, and various alcohols. Among these, gasoline is the predominant ignitable liquid accelerant encountered in forensic investigations. Common combustible household items, such as wicker and foam, can also accelerate fires depending on their usage. Investigators identify accelerants using trained detection dogs, irregular burn patterns, and laboratory chemical analysis, though gaseous accelerants like butane and propane leave no chemical residue.

title: Cash4Gold

Customers shipped items in pre-paid envelopes, after which Cash4Gold appraised the materials and mailed a payment offer that sellers could accept or decline within ten days.

title: OpenStack
summary:
OpenStack is a free, open-standard cloud computing platform primarily deployed as Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) in public and private clouds. Founded in 2010 as a joint project by Rackspace Hosting and NASA, it is managed by the Open Infrastructure Foundation and supported by hundreds of companies.

title: Apis (deity)

A calf matching specific physical markings was selected, housed in a temple, and worshiped as a living deity that provided oracles and healing. When an Apis died, it was mummified and given an expensive burial. Over sixty bulls were interred over 1,400 years, primarily in the Serapeum at Saqqara. 

After death, the bull became Osorapis (Osiris-Apis). To unite Greek and Egyptian subjects, Ptolemy I later promoted an anthropomorphic form named Serapis, a human-styled god whose cult eventually spread to Ancient Rome.

Piloted by Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon, the aircraft completed a 41-hour flight from Japan to a belly landing in East Wenatchee, Washington, having intentionally jettisoned its landing gear shortly after takeoff to conserve weight for fuel.
